neighbors.heading: nearer than a heartbeat
neighbors.text: Today Sukhmani said the One lives in every heart, ghat ghat, every clay jar. Muslims hear God's nearness in the Qur'an's own words: "We are nearer to him than his jugular vein." The verse says God already knows what a person's soul whispers to itself, before a word is spoken.
neighbors.difference: For Sikhs, the One's Light shines within every being. For Muslims, God is closer than anything, yet never dwells inside creation; He is near in knowing and care, and wholly other than what He made.
neighbors.shared: no one is ever as far from God as they feel.

neighbors.heading: the lord in the heart
neighbors.text: Today Sukhmani said God dwells in every heart, and so the langar seats everyone in the same rows. Hindus hear something close in the Bhagavad Gita. Near its end, Krishna tells Arjuna that the Lord dwells in the heart of all beings, turning them as if on a wheel by His power.
neighbors.difference: Sikhs speak of the One Light in every heart, the One who is never born and takes no incarnation. In the Gita it is Krishna, honored by many Hindus as God come in human form, who speaks of the Lord in the heart.
neighbors.shared: the stranger beside you carries the same light you do.

items.lessonTitle: Ashtpadi 23, salok: the ointment of wisdom

neighbors.heading: the eye arose
neighbors.text: Today the Guru's wisdom was an ointment for the eyes, and the darkness simply ended. Buddhists remember the Buddha's first teaching in a deer park. Describing his awakening, he says that about things never heard before, vision arose, knowledge, wisdom and true knowledge arose, and light arose.
neighbors.difference: In the salok, the Guru applies the ointment by God's grace. In the Buddha's teaching, the light comes through seeing the way things are for oneself, with no creator to grant it, though a teacher points the way.
neighbors.shared: the world was there all along; clear eyes let you see it.

neighbors.heading: now i see
neighbors.text: Today the Guru cleared the seeker's eyes, and the dark room filled with light. Christians remember a man born blind whom Jesus healed with clay on his eyes. Pressed with questions about who had healed him, he answered simply: "one thing I know, that, whereas I was blind, now I see."
neighbors.difference: In the salok, the ointment is the Guru's wisdom, clearing inner sight. In the Gospel, the healing is told as a real cure of a man's eyes by Jesus, whom Christians follow as the light of the world.
neighbors.shared: sometimes all you can say is, i see now.

neighbors.heading: out of the cave
neighbors.text: Today Guru Angad said a hundred moons and a thousand suns still leave us dark without the Guru. Plato told a story of people chained in a cave, taking shadows on the wall for the whole world. Someone has to turn one of them around and lead them, squinting, up into the sun.
neighbors.difference: For Sikhs, the light is the Guru, the Word teaching from within, carried by the Gurus and the Guru Granth Sahib. For Plato, the light is the Good, reached by reason, and any guide out of the cave is a fellow human.
neighbors.shared: plenty of light outside doesn't mean you can see.
neighbors.sources: Plato, Republic, Book VII, the allegory of the cave (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the light of life
neighbors.text: Today Guru Angad said the brightest sky can't reach the darkness the Guru lifts. Catholics hear Jesus in the Gospel: "I am the light of the world: he that followeth me, walketh not in darkness, but shall have the light of life." At the Easter Vigil, a single candle is carried into a dark church.
neighbors.difference: For Sikhs, the light is the Guru's Word, now the Guru Granth Sahib. For Catholics, the light is a person, Jesus Christ, God made man, met in the Church and the sacraments.
neighbors.shared: the light that matters most shows you which way to turn.

neighbors.heading: the wind keeps its place
neighbors.text: Today Guru Nanak sang that in awe the wind blows, the rivers run, and the sun keeps its course. Hindus have an old echo. The Taittiriya Upanishad says that from awe of the Supreme the wind blows and the sun rises, and fire, Indra and Death all go about their work.
neighbors.difference: In the Upanishad, the Supreme is Brahman, the ground of all, and the gods are honored powers within its order. In the salok, only the Formless is without fear; gods and heroes stand in awe with everyone else.
neighbors.shared: everything keeps faith with its place in a larger order.

neighbors.heading: fulfilling his word
neighbors.text: Today the salok said wind, rivers and fire all move in awe of the One. A psalm calls the whole of creation to praise, the sun and moon, the deep seas, and "stormy wind, fulfilling His word." Jews name the right response yirat shamayim, the awe of heaven, which keeps a life upright.
neighbors.difference: Sikhs hear the wind moving within hukam, the One's order. In the psalm, creation obeys the word of the God who made it, and for Jews, human awe takes shape in keeping the Torah.
neighbors.shared: awe is knowing where you belong, not being afraid.

neighbors.heading: lowliness of mind
neighbors.text: Today Guru Nanak called sweetness and humility the essence of every virtue: the side that bends low is the heavy one. Christians hear Paul writing to a church in Philippi: "in lowliness of mind let each esteem other better than themselves." He points to Jesus, who he says took the form of a servant.
neighbors.difference: For Sikhs, humility grows by remembering the Name and losing ego. For Christians, the pattern is Jesus himself, believed to be God who humbled himself to become human and die on a cross.
neighbors.shared: the one who bends low is often the one who holds the most.

neighbors.heading: walking gently
neighbors.text: Today the salok named two words, sweetness and humility, and called them the heart of goodness. The Qur'an draws a portrait of the faithful: they "walk upon the earth modestly, and when the foolish ones address them answer: Peace." Low in step, sweet in reply.
neighbors.difference: In the salok, humility is the weight on the scale that shows real value. In the Qur'an, it's a mark of servants of the Merciful, whose whole life is surrender to Allah.
neighbors.shared: a gentle answer can end a fight before it starts.

neighbors.heading: the bond of perfection
neighbors.text: Today young Nanak asked for a thread spun from compassion, contentment, restraint and truth. Saint Paul tells Christians to put on mercy, kindness, humility and patience like clothing, and then ties them all together: "above all these things have charity, which is the bond of perfection." Love is what holds the rest.
neighbors.difference: In the salok, compassion is the raw cotton everything else is spun from. For Catholics, charity is love poured into the heart by God, received in baptism, and it binds the other virtues.
neighbors.shared: goodness needs one strong strand to hold it together.

neighbors.heading: not by birth
neighbors.text: Today the salok asked what makes a sacred thread holy, and answered with compassion and truth. Buddhists remember the Buddha asking a similar question about the priestly class of his day. In the Dhammapada he says no one is a brahmin by birth, family or matted hair, but by truth and goodness.
neighbors.difference: Nanak spins his virtues into a thread of the soul for God. The Buddha's verse is about a person's conduct leading toward freedom from suffering, with no creator in view.
neighbors.shared: what's inside a person counts more than what they wear.

neighbors.heading: i will wake the dawn
neighbors.text: Today the Asa di Var was sung in the hours around sunrise, in amrit vela. A psalm wants to beat the sun up: "awake, psaltery and harp; I will awake the dawn." Many Jews pray Shacharit, the morning service, every day, and the Talmud praises those who time their prayer to the sunrise.
neighbors.difference: Sikhs sing the Guru's hymns with the ragis, often over hours. Jewish morning prayer is a fixed order of blessings, psalms and the Shema, said in Hebrew, ideally with a minyan of ten.
neighbors.shared: the first hour of the day can belong to something bigger.

neighbors.heading: a cheerful invitation
neighbors.text: Today the var was sung while the sky went from black to gray to gold. Thoreau, living by a pond, wrote of the morning too: "Every morning was a cheerful invitation to make my life of equal simplicity, and I may say innocence, with Nature herself." He rose early and bathed in the pond.
neighbors.difference: In amrit vela, Sikhs rise to remember the true Name and sing the Guru's words. Thoreau met the dawn as a fresh start, with nature as his teacher, not a fixed prayer.
neighbors.shared: before the noise starts, the day is still yours to shape.
neighbors.sources: Henry David Thoreau, Walden, "Where I Lived, and What I Lived For" (1854)

neighbors.heading: an atom's weight
neighbors.text: Today the Katak stanza said we earn what our deeds earn, and no one else is to blame. The Qur'an puts it in the smallest unit it can: "whoso doeth good an atom's weight will see it then, and whoso doeth ill an atom's weight will see it then." Nothing done is lost.
neighbors.difference: Sikh teaching holds deeds and the Guru's grace together, across the round of births. In Islam, every deed is weighed on one Day of Judgment, before a just and merciful God, after one life.
neighbors.shared: owning what you did is where every repair begins.

neighbors.heading: as you act
neighbors.text: Today Guru Arjan's Katak stanza said we reap what we did, so blame no one. Hindus call that law karma. An old Upanishad says that as a person acts, so they become: doing good, they become good; doing harm, they become harmful. Desire shapes will, will shapes deeds, and deeds shape who we are.
neighbors.difference: Sikhs and Hindus share the word karma. In the Sikh stanza, the deepest deed is forgetting the Lord, and the Guru's mercy can still reach the field. Hindu schools describe release in their own ways: knowledge, devotion or selfless action.
neighbors.shared: the field you stand in is the one you planted.

items.lessonTitle: The world as a wall of sand

neighbors.heading: like a dream
neighbors.text: Today the ninth Guru said this creation passes like a dream in the night, or a cloud's shadow on a field. A well-known Buddhist verse closes the Diamond Sutra the same way: see everything made like a dream, an illusion, a bubble, a shadow, dew, a flash of lightning. Look at it that way, it says.
neighbors.difference: For Sikhs, the passing world is still the Lord's creation, and the steady thing is His shelter. Buddhists see impermanence as the nature of everything conditioned, with no creator behind them, and seeing it clearly loosens suffering.
neighbors.shared: hold what you love gently; it was never yours to grip.

neighbors.heading: a vapour
neighbors.text: Today the Guru called the body a dream that comes in the night. Christians hear James, who warned people making big plans for next year: "For what is your life? It is even a vapour, that appeareth for a little time, and then vanisheth away." Instead, he says, add "if the Lord will."
neighbors.difference: The Guru points to the Lord's shelter and the Name as what lasts. For Christians, what lasts is life with God through Christ, and they hope for the resurrection of the body, not only release from it.
neighbors.shared: plans are good; holding them lightly is better.

neighbors.heading: not the thing, the opinion
neighbors.text: Today the ninth Guru drew a portrait of someone who, in pain, doesn't crown pain king. The Stoic teacher Epictetus, once a slave, taught nearly the same steadiness: "Men are disturbed not by the things which happen, but by the opinions about the things." Our judgments, he said, are ours to work on.
neighbors.difference: For the Guru, the steady one has merged with the Lord, like water into water. For Epictetus, steadiness comes from reason, sorting what is in our power from what isn't.
neighbors.shared: you can feel the storm without letting it steer.

neighbors.heading: health or sickness
neighbors.text: Today the hymn praised the one who sees gold and dust alike, unmoved by praise or blame. Saint Ignatius of Loyola asks the same of people making his Spiritual Exercises: be free inside, not preferring health to sickness, riches to poverty, honor to dishonor, a long life to a short one, for the sake of God.
neighbors.difference: The Guru describes one who has merged with the Lord. Ignatius calls this freedom indifference: choosing whatever best serves the purpose he names, to praise, reverence and serve God, and so be saved.
neighbors.shared: freedom inside lets you choose well when life shifts.
neighbors.sources: Ignatius of Loyola, Spiritual Exercises, Principle and Foundation (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: no one shrinks from them
neighbors.text: Today the ninth Guru called someone wise who frightens no one and fears no one. Hindus hear a close match in the Gita. Krishna names who is dear to him: the one from whom the world doesn't shrink, and who doesn't shrink from the world, free of joy, envy, fear and agitation.
neighbors.difference: In the salok, the fearless one begins to resemble the One who is nirbhau and nirvair, without fear or enmity. In the Gita, it's a mark of the devotee whom Krishna, God for many Hindus, holds dear.
neighbors.shared: courage and gentleness can live in the same person.

neighbors.heading: whom shall i fear
neighbors.text: Today the salok asked for a person who gives fear to no one and takes it from no one. The Torah pairs two ideas in one verse: "ye shall not wrong one another; but thou shalt fear thy God." And a psalm finishes the thought: "The LORD is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear?"
neighbors.difference: Sikhs aim to become fearless, like the Formless. In Judaism, fear of God, reverent awe, stays at the center of a life, and the psalm finds in God freedom from every other fear.
neighbors.shared: a heart steady in the right place frightens no one.

neighbors.heading: call on the name
neighbors.text: Today the Name was a boat across a stormy ocean. Christians often call on a name too. Paul writes: "For whosoever shall call upon the name of the Lord shall be saved." The Gospels tell of Jesus asleep in a boat in a storm, woken by frightened friends, and the sea going calm.
neighbors.difference: In Sikh teaching the boat is Naam, remembering the formless One. For Christians the name is Jesus, believed to be the Son of God, and being saved means life with God through his death and rising.
neighbors.shared: in the worried hour, you don't have to swim alone.

neighbors.heading: in the name of allah
neighbors.text: Today the ninth Guru said the Name carries a person across the terrifying sea. The Qur'an tells of Noah loading the ark as the flood began. He told those with him: "Embark therein! In the name of Allah be its course and its mooring." Muslims begin a journey, a meal, almost anything, with bismillah, in the name of Allah.
neighbors.difference: For Sikhs, the boat is simran, remembering the Name across the round of births. In Islam, saying Allah's name is a believer's trust in one God, whose mercy is hoped for on the Last Day.
neighbors.shared: a name said in trust can carry you through the waves.

neighbors.heading: unto dust
neighbors.text: Today the salok said whatever is born will pass, today or tomorrow, so sing. Catholics hear it on Ash Wednesday, when ashes are pressed on foreheads with words from Genesis: "for dust thou art, and into dust thou shalt return." Then comes Lent, forty days to turn back toward God.
neighbors.difference: For Sikhs, the passing is hukam, and the Name is what stays. Catholics believe the dust is not the end: they hope for the resurrection of the body, through Christ's own rising at Easter.
neighbors.shared: knowing life is short is a reason to spend it well.

neighbors.heading: the last words
neighbors.text: Today the ninth Guru said whatever has sprung up will perish, and the date is the only open question. Buddhists remember the Buddha's last words, spoken as he lay dying: "Decay is inherent in all component things! Work out your salvation with diligence!" Passing, and so, effort.
neighbors.difference: The Guru answers passing with praise of the Lord and the Name. The Buddha answers it with diligent practice, walking the path to the end of suffering, with no creator in view.
neighbors.shared: the frost is coming; pick the tomatoes and share them.

neighbors.heading: he laid his hands
neighbors.text: Today the Ardas remembered Guru Nanak handing the Guruship to his disciple Lehna, by fitness, not by blood. Jews remember Moses and his student Joshua: "Joshua the son of Nun was full of the spirit of wisdom; for Moses had laid his hands upon him." The Mishnah traces the chain: Moses received the Torah and handed it to Joshua.
neighbors.difference: For Sikhs, the same light passed from Nanak to Angad, and later to the Guru Granth Sahib. In Judaism, Moses stays unique among prophets; what passes on is the Torah and its teaching, not Moses himself.
neighbors.shared: a good teacher is measured by who carries it next.

neighbors.heading: from my grandfather
neighbors.text: Today the Ardas named the Gurus one by one, a teacher, then a student who became a teacher. The emperor Marcus Aurelius began his private notebook the same way: a list of those who formed him. From his grandfather, good morals; from his mother, a simple way of living; from teacher after teacher, what each gave.
neighbors.difference: Sikhs remember the Gurus as one divine light in ten bodies. Marcus thanks ordinary people for ordinary gifts, and the gods for the good fortune of having known them.
neighbors.shared: you're made of everyone who took the time to teach you.

neighbors.heading: forgive and overlook
neighbors.text: Today the Ardas honored those who saw others' faults and chose to make them unseen. The Qur'an asks the same of people with a real grievance: "Let them forgive and show indulgence. Yearn ye not that Allah may forgive you?" A hadith adds that whoever covers a brother's fault, Allah will cover theirs.
neighbors.difference: In the Ardas, overlooking sits beside the sword: let the slight go, but stand against cruelty. In the Qur'an, forgiving is mercy from people who hope for Allah's mercy, and justice against wrong is upheld too.
neighbors.shared: some of the best things people do are invisible on purpose.
neighbors.sources: Qur'an 24:22 (Pickthall 1930) · Sahih Muslim, on covering faults (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: no fault-finding
neighbors.text: Today the Ardas remembered people who saw clearly, and let it go. Hindus find the same habit in the Gita's list of divine qualities: gentleness, forgiveness, compassion toward all beings, and an aversion to finding fault. Krishna counts it among the marks of someone born with a divine nature.
neighbors.difference: Sikhs ask God's help to live as those Ardas heroes did, in a community that also protects. In the Gita, these qualities are part of a person's nature and dharma, leading toward freedom.
neighbors.shared: a family runs on people who decide not to keep score.

neighbors.heading: faith is the seed
neighbors.text: Today the Ardas asked for trust and faith as gifts. Buddhists talk about faith too, saddha, confidence in the Buddha's way. A farmer once mocked the Buddha for not plowing, and the Buddha answered that he did plow: faith is his seed, discipline the rain, wisdom his yoke and plow.
neighbors.difference: In the Ardas, faith is a gift asked of God. In the early Buddhist texts, faith is confidence a person tests and grows by practice, with no God who grants it.
neighbors.shared: trust grows best when you keep tending it.

neighbors.heading: the gift of god
neighbors.text: Today the Ardas asked for faith as daan, a gift freely given, not earned. Many Christians speak of faith that way. Paul writes: "For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God." Many Christians pray for more of it, like the father in the Gospel: help my unbelief.
neighbors.difference: Sikhs ask for faith alongside discipline, uncut hair and discernment, the gifts of a Sikh life. For Christians, faith is trust in Jesus Christ, and grace through him is the gift that saves.
neighbors.shared: faith can be something you ask for, not only something you have.

neighbors.heading: the swarm and the bee
neighbors.text: Today the Ardas widened at its end: by Your will, good for all. Marcus Aurelius, writing in his private notebook, kept coming back to the same idea, that we are made for one another. One line says it in a single picture: "That which is not good for the swarm, neither is it good for the bee."
neighbors.difference: The Ardas asks good for all of God, by His will. Marcus reasons it out: a person is part of one human community, so his own good can't be separated from everyone's.
neighbors.shared: your good and everyone's good are tied together.

neighbors.heading: for all men
neighbors.text: Today the Ardas ended with good for all, no one left off the list. Catholics pray that wide at Mass, in the prayers of the faithful, following Saint Paul: "I desire therefore, first of all, that supplications, prayers, intercessions, and thanksgivings be made for all men." Rulers, strangers, enemies, the whole world.
neighbors.difference: Sikhs close with chardi kala, rising spirits through the Name, and ask good for all in God's will. Catholics pray through Christ, whom they believe gave himself for all people.
neighbors.shared: a prayer can end by widening to include everyone.

neighbors.heading: offered first
neighbors.text: Today Sikhs paused before food to thank the Giver. Some Hindu families say a Gita verse before eating: the offering is Brahman, the food is Brahman, offered by Brahman into the fire of Brahman. In temples and homes, food is often offered to God first, then shared as prasad, a blessing.
neighbors.difference: Sikhs say Ardas over food, in the gurdwara before the Guru Granth Sahib, with no image or idol. Hindus often offer food before a sacred image, a murti, where many feel God is present to receive it.
neighbors.shared: a meal given thanks for is hard to eat in a rush.

neighbors.heading: bless after you eat
neighbors.text: Today the Ardas made a pause before the plate. Jews bless God before eating: over bread, for bringing forth bread from the earth. And the Torah adds a blessing after: "thou shalt eat and be satisfied, and bless the LORD thy God for the good land which He hath given thee."
neighbors.difference: Sikhs pray an Ardas, in their own words or a few set lines, before the meal. Jewish blessings are fixed words, said before each kind of food, and the longest grace comes after the meal, once you're full.
neighbors.shared: food is a gift, so the table starts with thanks.
neighbors.sources: Deuteronomy 8:10 (JPS 1917) · the blessing over bread, hamotzi (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the whole world
neighbors.text: Today Guru Nanak imagined a palace of pearls and prayed only not to forget. Jesus asked a question his followers still carry: "For what is a man profited, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul?" He also told of a rich man who built bigger barns and forgot what mattered.
neighbors.difference: Guru Nanak doesn't ask for less, only to remember the Giver. Jesus also called some followers to leave everything and follow him, and Christians honor both householders and those who give it all away.
neighbors.shared: a beautiful life can still make you forget the one who gave it.

neighbors.heading: let it not distract
neighbors.text: Today the shabad asked that no palace or throne make the Name slip from mind. The Qur'an gives the same warning to believers: "Let not your wealth nor your children distract you from remembrance of Allah." It doesn't call wealth or children bad. It names the danger as forgetting.
neighbors.difference: For Sikhs, remembering is simran of the Name, all through the day. Muslims keep that remembrance, dhikr, with phrases like subhan Allah, and five set prayers a day turn them back to Allah.
neighbors.shared: good things are safest when you remember where they came from.

neighbors.heading: one father
neighbors.text: Today Guru Arjan sang: one Father, and we are all His children. The prophet Malachi asked his people almost the same question: "Have we not all one father? hath not one God created us?" And then the sharp part: why then does each of us despise his brother? Catholics see every person as made in God's image.
neighbors.difference: Guru Arjan's Father is the formless One, with no incarnation. Catholics know God as Father through Jesus, his Son, and speak of becoming God's adopted children through baptism.
neighbors.shared: the person you like least still sits at the same family table.
neighbors.sources: Malachi 2:10 (Douay-Rheims) · Catechism of the Catholic Church 1265 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: as a mother
neighbors.text: Today the shabad said we all belong to each other, with no one voted off. Buddhists reach the same circle with a different picture. The Metta Sutta asks: as a mother would guard her only child with her life, so let one keep a boundless heart toward all beings, above, below and across.
neighbors.difference: For Sikhs, we are siblings because we share one Father. Buddhism speaks of no creator; the kinship comes from a heart of loving-kindness that a person grows until it leaves no one out.
neighbors.shared: nobody has to earn a place in the family.

neighbors.heading: one flesh
neighbors.text: Today the fourth round closed the wedding, and Sikhs remembered: one light in two bodies. Jews read their own picture in Genesis: a man "shall cleave unto his wife, and they shall be one flesh." At many Jewish weddings the bride circles the groom under the chuppah, and seven blessings are sung.
neighbors.difference: Sikhs read the laavan on two levels, a marriage and a soul's journey to God, sealed by circling the Guru Granth Sahib. A Jewish marriage is a covenant between two people, made with a ring and a written ketubah.
neighbors.shared: a wedding is a walk you start together and keep walking.

neighbors.heading: spaces in your togetherness
neighbors.text: Today the fourth round ended in sahaj, the ease of two lives at rest together. Kahlil Gibran, writing about marriage in The Prophet, adds a gentle balance: "let there be spaces in your togetherness." Two pillars hold up one temple, he says, standing apart.
neighbors.difference: For Sikhs, the couple becomes one light in two bodies, and the union points toward God. Gibran prizes the closeness and also the space, so each stays whole.
neighbors.shared: love can be one light and still leave room to breathe.

neighbors.heading: the most beautiful names
neighbors.text: Today Guru Arjan sang Ram and Khuda, Kareem and Raheem, in one shabad. The Qur'an has its own word on names: "Cry unto Allah, or cry unto the Beneficent, unto whichsoever ye cry (it is the same). His are the most beautiful names." Muslims learn many of them: the Merciful, the Generous, the Peace.
neighbors.difference: Guru Arjan's shabad sees Hindu and Muslim names pointing to one Lord. The Qur'an's verse is about the names Allah gives Himself; in Islam, God's names are learned from revelation.
neighbors.shared: the name you call on matters, and so does the one you're calling.

neighbors.heading: the wise call it many
neighbors.text: Today the shabad walked down a street where neighbors call God Ram, Khuda, Gusain, Allah. Hindus have an old line from the Rig Veda often quoted for the same spirit: truth is one, and the wise call it by many names. The hymn lists the names the poets of its day used.
neighbors.difference: Guru Arjan says what counts is recognizing the one Lord's hukam. Many Hindus honor that one truth through many forms and images of God, which Sikhs do not worship.
neighbors.shared: a neighbor's prayer deserves your respect, even in other words.

neighbors.heading: chanted at the bedside
neighbors.text: Today a shabad sung for a sick friend was a gift. Buddhists keep that custom too. A sutta tells of the elder Mahakassapa lying ill, and the Buddha coming to recite the seven factors of awakening for him; the elder recovered. Theravada monks still chant protective verses, paritta, for the sick.
neighbors.difference: Sikhs sing the Guru's own Word and end with Ardas to God. Buddhist chanting recalls the Buddha's teaching, and its strength is in the truth and goodwill of the words, not a prayer to a creator.
neighbors.shared: when you don't know what to say, you can sing.

neighbors.heading: sing psalms
neighbors.text: Today Sikh families gathered with kirtan around someone ill. A letter in the New Testament gives Christians the same instinct: "Is any merry? let him sing psalms. Is any sick among you? let him call for the elders of the church; and let them pray over him." Many churches still bring hymns to hospital rooms.
neighbors.difference: Sikhs offer the Guru's company through the shabad, the Guru's living voice. Christians pray in the name of Jesus, and many churches anoint the sick with oil, as the same letter describes.
neighbors.shared: a shaky voice at a bedside is still a gift.

neighbors.heading: who you eat with
neighbors.text: Today Sikhs remembered Mata Khivi, mother of the langar, feeding everyone who came. The philosopher Seneca passed on a saying of Epicurus: think first about whom you'll eat and drink with, before what. A meal without a friend, he said, is the life of a lion or a wolf.
neighbors.difference: The langar feeds strangers, anyone at all, as service to the One. Epicurus valued the table for friendship, a circle chosen with care, as part of a calm and happy life.
neighbors.shared: a shared meal feeds more than the body.

neighbors.heading: you gave me to eat
neighbors.text: Today the langar's open kitchen came from Mata Khivi at Khadur. Catholics count feeding the hungry first among the corporal works of mercy, from Jesus's own words: "For I was hungry, and you gave me to eat." In the same story, he says what's done for the least is done for him.
neighbors.difference: Sikhs serve langar to everyone as seva, seeing the One's light in every guest. Catholics feed the hungry as if feeding Christ himself, who they believe is present in the poor.
neighbors.shared: an open kitchen says, you belong here.

neighbors.heading: the joints of the day
neighbors.text: Today the daily banis framed the day: praise before dawn, Rehras at dusk, Sohila at bedtime. Some Hindus keep sandhya vandana, prayers at the meeting points of the day, dawn, noon and dusk. At its heart is the Gayatri mantra from the Rig Veda, asking the light to inspire our minds.
neighbors.difference: Sikh Nitnem is a set of the Gurus' hymns, read by anyone. Sandhya is a Vedic rite with water and mantra, traditionally kept by those given the sacred thread, while other Hindus keep their own home prayer.
neighbors.shared: a day held between prayers feels held all the way through.

neighbors.heading: lying down, rising up
neighbors.text: Today Sikhs looked back on a day framed in words, from amritvela to Kirtan Sohila. Jews frame the day too. The Shema tells them to speak God's words "when thou liest down, and when thou risest up," and many say it morning and night, with a bedtime Shema before sleep.
neighbors.difference: Sikh Nitnem is the hymns of the Gurus, in Punjabi and older tongues. Jewish prayer centers on the Shema and the Amidah, in Hebrew, three services a day.
neighbors.shared: the first and last words of a day can be the same.

neighbors.heading: hid in mine heart
neighbors.text: Today Sikhs chose one line from the year to carry. Christians have a long habit of the same thing: learning a verse by heart. A psalm says why: "Thy word have I hid in mine heart, that I might not sin against thee." Many churches still give children a memory verse to learn each week.
neighbors.difference: Sikhs take the hukamnama as the living Guru's word for the day. Christians read Scripture as God's word that points to Jesus Christ, whom they call the Word made flesh.
neighbors.shared: a line kept by heart is there at the red light.

neighbors.heading: easy to remember
neighbors.text: Today the lesson asked for one line of bani, carried and turned over for months. Muslims memorize the Qur'an, some all of it, many children a few short surahs. A verse repeats like a refrain: "And in truth We have made the Qur'an easy to remember; but is there any that remembereth?"
neighbors.difference: Sikhs treat the Guru Granth Sahib as the living Guru and read a hymn as the day's order. Muslims hold the Qur'an as Allah's own word, recited in Arabic, word for word.
neighbors.shared: words you carry inside keep opening as you grow.
